skill.description: Guides Caffeine developers through Google Calendar OAuth, event listing, event creation, availability checks, token refresh, and required frontend routes.
skill.summary: Build per-user Google Calendar integrations for Caffeine apps with OAuth 2.0 PKCE and generated Motoko clients.
skill.author: caffeinelabs

security_audit.summary: All 322 static findings are false positives caused by Markdown formatting, documented URLs, fixed local references, ellipses, and ordinary identifier text. The skill contains no executable scripts, command substitution, uncontrolled filesystem operations, reconnaissance, or prompt injection. One semantic finding remains: the canonical implementation defaults to a full Calendar scope that exceeds its demonstrated event and availability operations.

remediation.issue: The canonical example requests full Calendar access for event and availability operations.
remediation.suggestion: Default to the narrowest event, availability, or read-only scopes that support enabled features. Require and explain full Calendar access only for calendar-level management.

content.value_statement: Google Calendar integrations require careful OAuth, token, and time handling. This skill provides a Motoko recipe for authenticated event access, availability checks, and callback routing.
actual_capabilities: Provides pinned dependency commands for the Calendar client, Google OAuth, and Caffeine authorization packages.
Implements per-user OAuth 2.0 PKCE with admin-managed credentials and caller-scoped token storage.
Lists upcoming events and creates events on the signed-in user's primary calendar.
Queries FreeBusy and calculates availability with offset-aware RFC 3339 helpers.
Refreshes an expired access token once after an HTTP 401 response.
Defines admin settings, OAuth callback, connection status, event list, and event creation interfaces.
limitations: The recipe targets Caffeine apps using Motoko and Internet Computer dependencies.
An administrator must configure Google Cloud credentials and enable the Calendar API.
Additional Calendar operations require adaptation, authorization review, and application tests.
The canonical example requests broad Calendar read and write access.

use_cases.title: Add Personal Calendar Features
use_cases.description: Create a Caffeine app that connects each user, lists upcoming events, and creates events on the primary calendar.

use_cases.title: Build Availability Scheduling
use_cases.description: Query busy periods and present accurate free slots using offset-aware time calculations.

use_cases.title: Unify Gmail and Calendar Access
use_cases.description: Share one Google OAuth flow, credential set, callback route, and token record across both services.

prompt_templates.title: Set Up the Connector
prompt_templates.prompt: Add Google Calendar to my Caffeine app. Include authentication, admin credential settings, OAuth callback handling, upcoming events, and event creation.
prompt_templates.scenario: Beginner setup for a new calendar-enabled app.

prompt_templates.title: Create an Availability Picker
prompt_templates.prompt: Build a 30-minute availability picker for seven days. Use FreeBusy, offset-aware RFC 3339 parsing, and the signed-in user's calendar.

prompt_templates.title: Review OAuth Security
prompt_templates.prompt: Review my Google Calendar OAuth flow. Verify PKCE, state validation, exact callback handling, caller-scoped tokens, one refresh retry, and non-replicated requests.

prompt_templates.title: Combine Google Services
prompt_templates.prompt: Refactor my Gmail and Calendar connectors into one Google OAuth connection. Share credentials, token state, callback routing, and the required scope union.
prompt_templates.scenario: Advanced architecture for a multi-service app.

output_examples.input: Add Google Calendar with event listing and creation to my Caffeine app.
output_examples.output: A build plan covering authentication, admin settings, callback routing, event listing, event creation, dependencies, and token refresh.

output_examples.input: Show free 30-minute slots for the next work week.
output_examples.output: An availability workflow using FreeBusy, offset-aware timestamps, and busy-period subtraction before event creation.

output_examples.input: Combine my existing Gmail and Calendar integrations.
output_examples.output: A shared OAuth architecture with one settings page, one callback route, one connection record, and combined scopes.

best_practices: Request the narrowest Google scopes that support the enabled calendar features.
Keep client secrets and user tokens in caller-scoped canister state, never in browser storage.
Register the exact callback URI, validate state, and await actor readiness before completing OAuth.
anti_patterns: Do not replace the generated clients with raw unauthenticated HTTP requests.
Do not return access tokens, refresh tokens, client secrets, or complete connection records to the frontend.
Do not calculate availability from event lists when the FreeBusy endpoint meets the requirement.

faq.question: Can this skill list and create Google Calendar events?
faq.answer: Yes. The canonical recipe lists upcoming events and creates events on the signed-in user's primary calendar.

faq.question: Does every user need to sign in?
faq.answer: Yes. Calendar connections and tokens are stored separately for each authenticated caller.

faq.question: Who configures the Google OAuth credentials?
faq.answer: An application administrator enters the Google Web client ID and secret through an admin-only settings page.

faq.question: Which Google Calendar scope should I request?
faq.answer: Choose the narrowest scope that supports your features. The canonical full Calendar scope should be reduced when calendar-level management is unnecessary.

faq.question: How does the skill calculate availability?
faq.answer: It queries FreeBusy, parses offset-aware RFC 3339 times, and removes overlapping busy intervals from candidate slots.

faq.question: Can Gmail and Calendar share one Google connection?
faq.answer: Yes. The skill describes one credential set, scope union, callback route, and caller-scoped token record for both services.
